clue.text: Constant guest at iconic shows

indicators.note: to show something is to put it on display, so the clue words display a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters run consecutively across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A regular visitor turns up at every famous show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constant guest' reads as one phrase about a frequent visitor, but 'Constant' alone is the definition and the guest is only part of the hiding place: gueST AT IConic.
explanation.definitionFit: Static describes something unchanging or fixed, which is what constant means as an adjective.

clue.text: Difficulties avoiding eastern junks

indicators.note: whatever is avoided is kept out, so one letter is left out of the word

parts.note: a scrape is an awkward predicament, so difficulties are scrapes
E is the standard abbreviation for east or eastern

explanation.surface: Trouble is kept clear of the Chinese sailing boats in the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eastern junks' paints Chinese sailing ships, but 'junks' is a verb meaning throws away. SCRAPES loses its E to leave SCRAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrap something is to discard it as useless, the same as to junk it; both verbs are third person singular.

clue.text: Alien finally invading this galaxy could be Armageddon

indicators.note: something alien is strange and unfamiliar, so the letters appear in an unfamiliar order
the clue sets up an equation: the answer plus one letter could be the last word, so that letter must be taken away from it

parts.note: the last word of the clue, taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word it sits beside

parts.note: the final letter of this word

explanation.surface: If an alien invaded our neighbouring galaxy it might mean the end of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite clue with the definition in the middle: the galaxy with G added could become Armageddon, so take G from ARMAGEDDON and rearrange the rest. Read as a whole, the sentence also describes an alien invasion.
explanation.definitionFit: Andromeda is the large spiral galaxy nearest our Milky Way, so it is named here as a particular galaxy.

clue.text: Lady's last to leave exterior pub areas for interior

indicators.note: a letter that leaves goes out of the phrase and takes no part in the answer

parts.note: the yards outside an inn are its outdoor areas

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word, the 's marking possession

explanation.surface: A woman heads out from the beer garden to drink inside instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a drinker moving indoors; actually INN YARDS loses the Y at the end of 'Lady' to give INNARDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Innards are the inner parts of a body or machine, so the word names the inside, the interior.

clue.text: Improved film ratings with excellent edition

parts.note: U (universal) and PG (parental guidance) are British film certificates
rad is slang for excellent
ED is the abbreviation for edition

explanation.surface: A film's ratings went up after a superb new release.
explanation.walkthrough: U and PG are the British Board of Film Classification's two family-friendly certificates; RAD is American-flavoured slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: To upgrade something is to raise its standard, so a thing that has been upgraded has been made better.

clue.text: Chaos over in slate mine plastered with mud

parts.note: to slate a show is to pan it, criticising it harshly

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it
plastered is slang for very drunk, and a drunk's letters lurch out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Bedlam breaks out in a slate quarry when the workings get caked in mud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slate mine' looks like a quarry, but slate is a verb meaning criticise, and the mine belongs with the mud as material to be jumbled, the over going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Pandemonium is wild uproar and disorder, a near-exact synonym of chaos in everyday use.

clue.text: Cost to secure house with large entrance to living area

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so the outer word holds the others inside

parts.note: a rate is a charge or price
HO is the abbreviation for house
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: The fee for a house with a grand doorway into the lounge.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like an estate agent's listing with a big entrance hall; the definition is a hole in the wall, the doorway to a rat's home.
explanation.definitionFit: A rathole is the hole a rat uses to get into its nest, so it is the way into a rodent's home.

clue.text: Awe Romeo out of play receives

indicators.note: to receive is to take in, so one piece is taken inside the other

parts.note: in ball games a dead ball is one out of play
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Wonder that Romeo is cut from the play and the audience takes it well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Romeo out of play' suggests a deletion from Shakespeare, but 'out of play' is one unit meaning DEAD, which takes in R.
explanation.definitionFit: Dread is deep fear mixed with reverence, which overlaps with awe in its older sense of fearful respect.

clue.text: Extracting shelled crab parts having dinner

indicators.note: to part something is to split it open, so one piece pushes into another and divides it

parts.note: having dinner is dining

indicators.note: a shelled creature has had its outside removed, so only the middle letters stay

parts.note: the word without its outer letters

explanation.surface: Pulling the meat from a cracked crab while eating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crab parts' looks like a list of claws and legs, but 'parts' is a verb: the shelled crab splits DINING after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Draining means drawing off liquid or resources, a sense of extracting something until little remains.

clue.text: Gang infiltrated by copper remaining undisturbed

indicators.note: a group infiltrated by someone has that person working inside it

parts.note: a ring is a criminal gang, as in a smuggling ring
a DI, detective inspector, is a police officer, and copper is slang for one

explanation.surface: A criminal gang has an undercover police officer inside, still unsuspected.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper here is police slang, not the metal Cu. The definition uses the idiom 'let it ride', and a ship riding at anchor lies still.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter left riding is allowed to continue untouched, and a moored vessel riding at anchor stays put.

clue.text: Three articles by graduate source of scorn

indicators.note: by means next to, so the last piece is set alongside the earlier ones

parts.note: the English articles are a, an and the
an MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate degree holder

explanation.surface: A graduate writes three papers and earns nothing but contempt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests published papers; in crosswords it usually means the grammatical words A, AN and THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Anathema is something intensely detested, the thing a person regards with loathing and contempt.

clue.text: Course of instruction for golf almost completely full

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: pro means in favour of
Golf is G in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a room rammed with people is packed to capacity

explanation.surface: A golf course with lessons that is nearly fully booked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like a link word but supplies PRO. 'Rammed' is British slang for crowded.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme is a planned series of studies or activities, such as a degree programme or training scheme.

clue.text: Car appropriate to carry Republican, one of government office

indicators.note: to carry something is to bear it within, so one piece holds others

parts.note: the Mini is a classic small British car
to appropriate is to take for oneself, to steal
R is the abbreviation for Republican
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A suitable car to drive a Republican politician to government work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as the adjective suitable but is the verb meaning take; STEAL carries R and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Ministerial describes things relating to a minister, a holder of senior political office in a cabinet.

clue.text: Ancient Cockney's BGT judge

indicators.note: a Cockney, a working-class Londoner, traditionally drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: Amanda Holden is a long-serving judge on Britain's Got Talent

explanation.surface: A veteran talent-show judge described in a London accent.
explanation.walkthrough: BGT is Britain's Got Talent, a TV talent show; drop Holden's H the way a Cockney would.
explanation.definitionFit: Olden is an old-fashioned adjective for long past times, as in the olden days, so it means ancient.

clue.text: Argentine leader hosting relation, regular drinkers directly communicating

indicators.note: a host has guests inside the home, so the outer piece holds the others

parts.note: Juan Perón was President of Argentina
a son is a family relation
a toper is a habitual drinker

explanation.surface: Argentina's president hosts a relative and some heavy drinkers for frank talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Argentine leader' looks like a first-letter instruction for A, but it is the president, Perón.
explanation.definitionFit: Person-to-person describes contact made between individuals face to face, without any intermediary, so it is communication made directly.

clue.text: Casual pyrotechnist no pro and not natural

indicators.note: something casual is careless and haphazard, so the letters fall in no set order
no means without, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An amateur fireworks maker with no professional training and a fake air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casual pyrotechnist no pro' reads as a description of an amateur; the PRO is struck out of the word and the remaining nine letters rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Synthetic means made artificially by chemical process rather than occurring in nature, as with man-made fibres.

clue.text: Burns, perhaps, under crusted skin's protective covering

indicators.note: in a down entry, something under another piece sits below it, so it comes second

parts.note: a scab is the crust that forms over a wound
Robert Burns, Scotland's national poet, is known as the Bard; 'perhaps' marks him as one example of a poet

explanation.surface: Treating burns under a crusty layer of skin with a protective dressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burns' is capitalised at the start of the clue so it passes as injuries; it is the Scottish poet Robert Burns, a bard.
explanation.definitionFit: A scabbard is the sheath that holds a sword or dagger, a cover that protects the blade and the wearer.

clue.text: According to Spooner, source of eggs for Roald, novelist

indicators.note: William Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so two sounds change places here

parts.note: Roald Dahl wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory; his chickens would be Dahl's, and the D swaps for a CH sound
chickens lay eggs; the CH sound swaps for D

explanation.surface: Where the children's author Roald Dahl got his eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'Dahl's chickens' and swap the opening D and CH sounds to hear Charles Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens is the Victorian author of Oliver Twist and Great Expectations, an example of a writer of fiction.

clue.text: ALl sUCh fINDs completely uncovered by A girl

indicators.note: uncovering strips off the outside layer, so each word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: the inside of the word
the inside of the word
the inside of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: All the finds a girl uncovered on a dig.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals are the setter's visual nudge to the kept letters and carry no other wordplay; strip each word's ends, then add A.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucinda is a female first name, so it is one example of a name a girl might have.

clue.text: Like agreeable wine

parts.note: kind means pleasant and good-natured
red is a type of wine

explanation.surface: A wine that tastes pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' looks like a comparison or a verb, but it is an adjective meaning similar, as in kindred spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Kindred as an adjective means similar in nature or character, as in kindred spirits, which is like in its adjectival sense.

clue.text: Picked up knacks to make legwear

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a flair is a natural talent or knack

explanation.surface: Learning the skills needed to sew trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up knacks' sounds like learning skills, but 'picked up' is the sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Flares are trousers that widen from the knee, popular in the 1970s, so they are an item of clothing for the legs.

clue.text: Simple tree extraordinary in auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience listens, so the words count as heard

parts.note: the bay is a laurel tree
sick is youth slang for amazing or extraordinary

explanation.surface: A plain tree looks remarkable inside a concert hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bay sick' said quickly sounds like the answer; the slang SICK for brilliant is what makes 'extraordinary' work.
explanation.definitionFit: Basic means elementary and uncomplicated, stripped down to essentials, so it means plain or simple.

clue.text: Men swapping tips somewhere in America

indicators.note: a word's tips are its two ends, and swapping them puts each in the other's place

parts.note: men are males

explanation.surface: Waiters trading gratuities in a US town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' suggests gratuities, but it means the two end letters, which trade places.
explanation.definitionFit: Salem is a city in Massachusetts, famous for its witch trials, and also the capital of Oregon, so a place in the United States.

clue.text: Cheese pieces with temperature maintained in space by onboard computer

indicators.note: something maintained in another is kept inside it

parts.note: an em is a printer's space, the width of a letter M
HAL 9000 is the spaceship computer in the film 2001: A Space Odyssey
chess pieces are called men
T is the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: Bits of cheese kept chilled in space by the spacecraft's computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Space' and 'onboard computer' paint a spaceship, but space is the typesetter's measure, and the computer is the famous one from Kubrick's film.
explanation.definitionFit: Emmenthal is a Swiss hard cheese with large holes, so it is one example of a cheese.

clue.text: Regularly ignored bad talk against South Island

indicators.note: ignoring at regular intervals means skipping every other letter and keeping the rest

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters, with the odd ones skipped
anti means against
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Nasty gossip about a southern island is regularly ignored.
explanation.walkthrough: Atlantis is the legendary island said to have sunk beneath the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlantis is the mythical island described by Plato that sank into the ocean, so it is an example of an island.

clue.text: Bowl right beside case

indicators.note: beside sets two pieces next to each other without saying which side, so both orders must be tried

parts.note: a crate is a packing case
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A bowling case placed on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl' looks like a cricket or bowling verb, but it is a noun: a bowl-shaped hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: A crater is a bowl-shaped depression in the ground, and in ancient Greece a krater was a mixing bowl for wine.

clue.text: Cursed the Spanish embargo with bananas getting turned back

indicators.note: turning back sends everything the other way, so the letters run from the end to the start

parts.note: el is Spanish for the
an embargo is a ban on trade
bananas is slang for crazy

explanation.surface: Someone swears at Spain's trade embargo as banana shipments are sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' wants to be the fruit cargo, but it is slang for crazy, MAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Damnable means deserving condemnation or very annoying, so it is close to cursed as an angry adjective for something hateful.

clue.text: Rogue heartlessly dictates orders

indicators.note: something rogue behaves wildly and out of control, so the letters break ranks
without a heart means the central letters are cut out

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A heartless villain issues commands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictates' looks like the verb meaning gives orders, but it is the fodder: remove its middle TA and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An edict is an official decree issued by an authority, so edicts are commands or orders.
